t: 2858. Minimum Edge Reversals So Every Node Is Reachable
o: The underlying undirected graph is a tree; each directed edge may need reversing depending on the root. For a chosen root r, the answer is the number of edges pointing away from... precisely, edges that must be flipped so all paths lead outward from r: an edge (u→v) costs 0 if we travel u→v and 1 if v→u. Example 1 answers [1,1,0,2]; rooting at node 2 costs nothing since both edges leave it. Compute cost(root=0) with one DFS, then reroot: moving the root across an edge (p,c) changes the answer by +1 if the edge is p→c (now must be reversed) and −1 if c→p. O(n) total.
k: cost(r) = number of edges on the tree that point 'against' the outward orientation from r.
First DFS from node 0 accumulates cost; second pass reroots: ans[child] = ans[parent] ± 1 (+1 if edge parent→child, −1 if child→parent).
Everything is O(n); iterative DFS/BFS avoids stack overflow on chains of 1e5 nodes.

a.i: Root the tree at 0; during a DFS record each node's parent and the edge direction to its parent, accumulating cost from the root. Then process nodes in DFS order: ans[v] = ans[parent] + (1 if edge was parent→v else −1), since flipping the root across that edge trades one unit.
s: Iterative DFS from 0 computing cost[0] and parent/dir arrays.
Reroot in DFS order to fill all answers.
a.t: O(n) — two linear passes over the tree.

a.i: Identical idea using BFS instead of DFS: level-order guarantees parents precede children, so both the cost accumulation and the reroot propagation work in a single queue-driven flow.
s: BFS from 0 recording parent and edge direction.
ans via the same ±1 propagation in BFS order.

w: Rerooting (a.k.a. change-of-root) is the canonical technique — memorize the ±1 delta pattern. Pitfalls: recursion depth on path-shaped trees (always iterate), and getting the sign backwards (test on a 2-node chain: root at the tail needs 1 reversal). Follow-up: edge weights (reversal costs differ per edge), or answering queries that re-root dynamically.
